findings.title: Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time and fails open when env vars are unset
findings.body: The webhook secret check uses a plain `!==` string comparison between `req.headers[...]` and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Two problems: (1) it is vulnerable to timing attacks, so a remote attacker could theoretically recover the secret byte-by-byte; (2) if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset (empty string) and the attacker sends an empty header value, `undefined !== undefined` is false... actually `req.headers[...]` would be `undefined` and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` would be `undefined`, so `undefined !== undefined` is `false`, meaning the check passes and the endpoint is left open. Note `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` which is falsy when unset, so the 403 guard at line 19 does protect against the unset case — but the comparison should still use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) and explicitly reject when either value is missing, rather than relying on the indirect guard. Additionally, the header name is read from an env var (`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`) which an attacker-controlled deployment misconfiguration could weaken; the secret value itself must never be logged or echoed.

findings.title: Zod parse errors and JSON.parse throw unhandled 500s instead of 400s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31) and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (line 57) throw on invalid input. In a Next.js API route an uncaught throw results in an unhandled 500 with a stack trace potentially leaked to the caller, instead of a clean 400 Bad Request. A caller sending a malformed body or a payload that fails decryption/parsing gets a 500. Use `.safeParse` and return 400, and wrap the decrypt/parse in try/catch returning 400 'Invalid encrypted payload'.

findings.title: Decryption uses empty-string fallback key when CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unset
findings.body: `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` falls back to an empty string key. If the env var is accidentally unset in a deployment where `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` was computed at build time (it is a module-level constant evaluated once at import), the endpoint would attempt to decrypt attacker-supplied ciphertext with a known empty key. Depending on the `symmetricDecrypt` implementation this could either throw or, worse, succeed for payloads encrypted with an empty key, letting an attacker write arbitrary credential keys. The handler should explicitly verify `process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is present and non-empty before decrypting and return 500/403 otherwise.

findings.title: findFirst-then-create/update race can create duplicate credentials or lose updates
findings.body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then either `update` or `create` based on the result. Two concurrent webhook calls for the same user+app can both observe 'no credential' and both create, producing duplicate credentials (the schema apparently allows multiple credentials per user+app since the code comments 'Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id'). Conversely two concurrent updates can interleave. There is no transaction or unique constraint enforced here. This is a data-integrity risk: duplicate credentials for the same app/user cause ambiguous credential selection downstream (other code uses `findFirst`, so behavior becomes nondeterministic). Wrap in `prisma.$transaction` with serializable isolation, or add a unique constraint on (userId, appId) where appId is non-null and use upsert.

findings.title: Created credential is not validated against the app's credential schema and may overwrite team credentials semantics
findings.body: When creating a new credential the handler sets `key: keys` where `keys` is the raw `JSON.parse` of the decrypted payload — an unvalidated `any`. Unlike the OAuth callback paths (which validate via zod schemas like `googleCredentialSchema`), this webhook writes arbitrary JSON into `credential.key`. A malformed payload (e.g. missing `refresh_token`, wrong types) will be persisted and later crash or misbehave the CalendarService/VideoApiAdapter that parses it. The handler should validate `keys` against the app's credential schema (the app metadata should expose it) before persisting. Also note the update path (line 73-80) overwrites the entire `key`, discarding fields like `expiry_date`/`email` that some services rely on — it should merge or validate.

findings.title: Endpoint does not restrict HTTP method
findings.body: The handler does not check `req.method`. Any HTTP verb (GET, PUT, DELETE, ...) reaching this route will be processed as a credential write. A GET request with a valid secret in the header and a body would still mutate the database, and GET requests may be logged by proxies/caches with the secret header. Restrict to POST (return 405 otherwise).

findings.title: Credential sync endpoint is called over plain fetch with no authentication, TLS validation is implicit, and response is trusted blindly
findings.body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` POSTs `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to that endpoint and returns the raw `Response`. Problems: (1) there is no authentication on this outbound call — any party that can guess/observe the endpoint URL could... actually the endpoint is server-configured, so the risk is that the *response* is fully trusted: the sync endpoint returns the new access token, and callers write it directly into the credential. If the endpoint is misconfigured to an http:// URL or is compromised/MITM'd, an attacker can inject arbitrary access tokens into users' credentials (token substitution → account takeover of the third-party integration). (2) The response is never checked for `response.ok`; a 500 HTML error page would flow into `response.json()` downstream and throw confusing errors, or worse, in callers like HubSpot the raw response object is used as a token. The function should enforce https, check `response.ok`, and callers should validate the parsed body.

findings.title: Sync endpoint response shape mismatch: callers expect provider-shaped bodies, not the raw fetch Response
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `Response` object from the sync endpoint, but callers treat the return value inconsistently. In `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 94 the caller does `const token = res?.data;` — a fetch `Response` has no `.data`, so `token` is `undefined` and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError whenever the sync path is active. Similarly `office365calendar` passes the Response into `handleErrorsJson(response)` which expects a Response (ok there), but `hubspot` assigns the Response to `hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` off it — undefined. The sync endpoint contract (returning JSON with access_token/expiry) is incompatible with the provider SDK response shapes (`.res.data`, axios `.data`, etc.) that the non-sync path returns. The abstraction leaks: each caller must handle two different shapes. `refreshOAuthTokens` should normalize: parse the sync endpoint's JSON and return a provider-equivalent shape, or callers must branch on which path was taken.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses invalid zod index-signature syntax and will never validate as intended
findings.body: The schema declares `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` as if they were index signatures. In Zod, computed keys in an object literal are just literal property names (the string `"string"`... actually `z.string().toString()` evaluates to `"string"`), so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "string": number, ... }` — it requires a property literally named `"string"` of type number and does NOT act as a catch-all. As written, `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)` will fail for any real token response that lacks a numeric property named `string`, causing `parseRefreshTokenResponse` to throw 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' whenever credential sharing is enabled. The intent (passthrough with numeric expiry fields) needs `.passthrough()`/`.catchall()` or an explicit shape. This breaks the entire sync-refresh path for Google/Office365/Zoom/Salesforce.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is silently replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token', destroying the stored credential
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — the literal string. OAuth providers often omit `refresh_token` on refresh responses (returning a new one only occasionally), and the correct behavior is to KEEP the existing refresh token. Instead, this overwrites the stored credential's refresh token with the garbage string `"refresh_token"`. The next refresh attempt will send `refresh_token="refresh_token"` to the provider, which will reject it with `invalid_grant`, permanently bricking the user's integration until they re-install. Callers like `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` then persist this corrupted key via `prisma.credential.update`. The function must not fabricate a refresh token; it should leave it absent and let callers merge with the existing credential (as `salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` correctly does with `refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token`).

findings.title: Return type is inconsistent: throws on failure but callers also check `.success`, and the success value shape differs between branches
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` when parsing fails (line 21-23), yet callers such as `salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` (line 90-94) and `zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts` (line 104-110) and `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` (line 263-264) treat the return value as a zod SafeParse result and check `.success` / access `.data`. Since the function throws instead of returning `{ success: false }`, those `.success` checks are dead code and the `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` branch in Salesforce is unreachable — a parse failure surfaces as an uncaught exception instead of the intended rejection path. The contract is muddled: either return the SafeParseResult (never throw) or throw consistently and fix all callers. As written, error handling in callers is broken.

findings.title: Sync-path token refresh reads `.data` off a fetch Response, causing TypeError and breaking Google Calendar when credential sharing is enabled
findings.body: In `refreshAccessToken`, `refreshOAuthTokens(...)` returns either the provider SDK's `fetchTokens.res` (a GaxiosResponse with `.data`) or, when sync is enabled, a raw fetch `Response` (which has no `.data`). Line 94 does `const token = res?.data;` then line 95 `googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;`. On the sync path `token` is `undefined` and `token.access_token` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. This exception is caught by the surrounding try/catch (line 103), which checks `if (message !== "invalid_grant") return myGoogleAuth;` — so it silently returns the auth client with the OLD expired access token, and every subsequent Google Calendar API call fails with 401 until the credential is reinstalled. The sync path for Google Calendar is completely broken.

findings.title: HubSpot refresh treats fetch Response as HubspotToken; sync path corrupts credentials with undefined fields
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response`, but line 177 assigns it to `hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken` and line 192 reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` and line 202 `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` — all `undefined` on a Response object. Line 192 computes `expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = `NaN`, and the credential is updated with `key: hubspotRefreshToken as any` — persisting a Response-serialized object (or garbage) over the user's real HubSpot tokens, destroying the integration. Additionally `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(undefined)` breaks all subsequent API calls. The non-sync path returns the HubSpot SDK token object directly (not a Response), so the two branches have incompatible shapes.

findings.title: Lark refresh passes fetch Response into handleLarkError which expects a Response on the normal path but the sync path response body is never parsed correctly
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` on the sync path returns the raw `Response` from the sync endpoint, and line 84 passes it to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`. On the normal path `resp` is the Lark API `fetch` Response, so `handleLarkError` presumably calls `resp.json()`. The sync endpoint returns a minimal JSON `{ access_token, expiry }` (per the PR description: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date'), which lacks the Lark envelope `{ code, data: { refresh_token, refresh_expires_in, access_token, expires_in } }` that lines 86-96 read (`data.data.refresh_expires_in`, `data.data.refresh_token`, etc.). So even if parsing succeeds, `data.data` is undefined and the credential update writes `undefined` tokens, or `handleLarkError` throws. The Lark sync path cannot work with the documented sync-endpoint contract.

findings.title: Office365 refresh silently proceeds with unvalidated token data when parse fails
findings.body: Line 263-264: `const tokenResponse = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema); o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`. But `parseRefreshTokenResponse` THROWS on parse failure rather than returning `{success: false}` (see separate finding), so the `.success` check is dead. Worse, if it did return a failure result, the spread `...(false && ...)` spreads `false`, which is a no-op — so the code would continue with the OLD (expired) credentials and persist them, silently failing to refresh. The previous code logged the zod error; that logging was removed in this diff. A failed refresh now either throws an unhandled error or silently keeps expired tokens. The refresh result must be checked and an error thrown/logged when invalid.

findings.title: MS Teams refresh: sync path returns Response but handleErrorsJson expects Response — however the sync endpoint's minimal JSON lacks refresh_token, permanently overwriting it with undefined
findings.body: On the sync path, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint's `Response`. `handleErrorsJson<ITokenResponse>(response)` will parse its JSON body. Per the PR's stated contract, the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry — no `refresh_token`. Line 84-95 then computes `expiry_date` from `expires_in` (which the minimal schema in `parseRefreshTokenResponse` treats as a generic number property, so it may be absent → `expiry_date = Date.now() + 0`) and writes `key: responseBody` to the database. The stored credential loses `refresh_token`, `email`, `scope`, `token_type`, etc. The next refresh reads `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token` = undefined and sends `refresh_token=undefined` to Microsoft, which rejects it — permanently breaking the Teams integration. The refresh must merge the new access token into the existing credential and preserve the refresh token (as Salesforce does).

findings.title: Webex refresh: sync-path Response body lacks refresh_token_expires_in required by webexRefreshedTokenSchema, so validation always fails on sync path
findings.body: When sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint Response whose JSON (per contract) contains only access token + expiry. `handleWebexResponse` parses it, then line 88 validates with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` which requires `refresh_token: z.string()` and `refresh_token_expires_in: z.number()`. The minimal sync response has neither, so `parsedToken.success` is false and line 89-91 rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' — the Webex credential can never be refreshed via sync, and the rejection propagates up through `getToken()` breaking meeting creation. The schema for the sync path must make refresh_token optional and preserve the existing one.

findings.title: Zoom refresh: parseRefreshTokenResponse throws instead of returning SafeParseResult, making the `.success` check dead and changing error semantics
findings.body: Line 104: `const parsedToken = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema);` then line 108 `if (!parsedToken.success)`. But `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` on failure (it never returns `{success: false}`), so `parsedToken.success` is always `true` when the function returns, and the explicit rejection branch is unreachable. A malformed Zoom refresh response now surfaces as a thrown Error from `parseRefreshTokenResponse` rather than the intended `Promise.reject(new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"))` — functionally similar but the dead code indicates the contract mismatch (see separate finding on parseRefreshTokenResponse). Additionally, on the sync path the minimal response (access_token + expiry only) lacks `refresh_token`, `token_type: "bearer"`, and `scope`, so `zoomRefreshedTokenSchema` validation fails and Zoom sync refresh always errors.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin refresh passes credentialId (a number) as the userId argument to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: Line 85-94: `refreshOAuthTokens(async () => ..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter is `credentialId` (the credential's database id), but `refreshOAuthTokens`'s signature is `(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId: number | null)` and it sends `calcomUserId: userId.toString()` to the sync endpoint. The sync endpoint expects the Cal.com user id, not the credential id. The self-hoster's app store will look up the wrong user (or none) and return the wrong tokens — or fail. This is a data-integrity/security issue: tokens for user A could be written into user B's credential if ids collide across tables. The call should pass `credential.userId` (the CredentialPayload has `userId`), matching every other caller.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin refresh: sync-path Response has no `.data`, so tokenInfo.data is undefined and the credential update writes undefined
findings.body: On the sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response`, but line 96 reads `tokenInfo.data.error` and line 98 `tokenInfo.data.expires_in` — a Response has no `.data`, so `tokenInfo.data` is `undefined` and `tokenInfo.data.error` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'error')`. This exception is NOT caught (the try/catch was removed in this refactor — the old code had no try/catch either but the shape matched), so the refresh crashes and the Bigin integration breaks whenever sync is enabled. The non-sync path returns an axios response with `.data`. The two shapes are incompatible.

findings.title: Zoho CRM refresh: sync-path Response has no `.data`; tokenInfo.data is undefined and refresh silently no-ops or crashes
findings.body: Line 204-216: `refreshOAuthTokens` on the sync path returns a fetch `Response`, but line 217 reads `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` and line 219 `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.expiryDate = ...` / line 233 `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.access_token`. A Response has no `.data`, so `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is `undefined` and `!zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` throws TypeError, which IS caught by the try/catch at line 238 and merely logged (`this.log.error(e)`) — so the refresh silently fails, `this.accessToken` is never updated, and all subsequent Zoho CRM API calls use the stale/empty access token. The sync path for Zoho CRM is broken and fails silently.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes the token on EVERY getClient call and overwrites the credential, even when the access token is still valid
findings.body: The diff adds an unconditional `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", { grant_type: "refresh_token", ... })` at the top of `getClient`, followed by `prisma.credential.update`. Previously `getClient` just constructed a jsforce Connection from the stored credential (jsforce itself refreshes lazily when needed). Now every construction of the SalesforceCalendarService (which happens per booking/availability check) triggers a Salesforce token refresh and a DB write. Consequences: (1) massive increase in outbound calls and DB writes (performance/rate-limit risk — Salesforce refresh tokens can also be single-use/rotating, so concurrent refreshes can invalidate each other); (2) the update at line 96-99 writes `{ ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token }` — but `accessTokenParsed.data` from the strict `salesforceTokenSchema` does NOT include `instance_url`... actually the schema requires `instance_url`, ok — but it drops any extra fields and, critically, if the refresh fails (`!response.ok`) it throws HttpError 400 which breaks all Salesforce operations; (3) there is no expiry check — a valid token is refreshed anyway. The refresh should only happen when the token is expired, and ideally reuse the `refreshOAuthTokens` helper for consistency.

findings.title: Salesforce error check uses `response.statusText !== "OK"` instead of `!response.ok`
findings.body: Line 86: `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError({ statusCode: 400, message: response.statusText });`. `Response.statusText` for a successful fetch is typically the empty string `""` (fetch spec: statusText is often empty for HTTP/2 and not guaranteed to be "OK"), so this condition is true even for successful responses and throws a 400 with an empty message — breaking Salesforce entirely. It should be `if (!response.ok)`. (Also note the jsforce Connection constructed at line 101 uses `credentialKey.access_token` — the OLD token — not the freshly refreshed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so even when the refresh succeeds the client is built with a stale token.)

findings.title: Salesforce jsforce Connection is built with the stale access token, not the freshly refreshed one
findings.body: Lines 101-108 construct `new jsforce.Connection({ ..., accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token })` using `credentialKey` (the credential as loaded at construction time), even though lines 75-99 just fetched a NEW access token (`accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`) and persisted it. The connection therefore uses the old (possibly expired) access token. jsforce will attempt its own refresh using `refreshToken`, which may work, but if the Salesforce refresh token rotates on use (Salesforce can invalidate old refresh tokens), the just-used refresh token in the DB update (line 98 keeps the old refresh_token) may already be invalid, and the connection's token is stale. The Connection should be built with `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string-or-undefined value, not a boolean, and is truthy-checked inconsistently
findings.body: `export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` evaluates to `string | undefined` (the value of the second env var when both are set, or `undefined`/empty string). It is used in boolean contexts (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`, `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT)`) which works, but: (1) if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=""` (empty string, as shipped in `.env.example` with `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=""`), the expression is `"" && ...` = `""` (falsy) — ok; but (2) the exported value leaks into client bundles potentially (constants.ts is imported widely) exposing whether the secret is set (not the value, but still); (3) more importantly, the webhook handler at `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` line 19 relies on this module-level constant, which is evaluated at import time — if env vars are loaded after module evaluation (e.g., in some Next.js runtime configurations), the flag could be stale. It should be an explicit boolean: `!!(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` and ideally the handler should read the env vars directly at request time.

findings.title: appStoreMetadata lookup uses app.slug from DB but credential is written with appMetadata.slug — mismatch for apps whose DB slug differs from metadata slug
findings.body: The handler looks up `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug: reqBody.appSlug } })` and then `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]`. It then writes the credential with `appId: appMetadata.slug` and `type: appMetadata.type`. If the DB `App.slug` differs from the metadata slug (e.g. DB stores `google-calendar` but metadata key is `google-calendar` — fine; but for apps like `msteams` vs `office365video`, or `zoom` vs `zoomvideo`), the credential's `appId`/`type` may not match what the app's service code queries for. The lookup should be done directly on `appStoreMetadata[reqBody.appSlug]` and the DB app check should be a secondary validation, or the code should assert `app.slug === appMetadata.slug`. As written, a webhook for slug `msteams` would find the DB app `msteams` but `appStoreMetadata["msteams"]` — if the metadata key is `office365video` — returns undefined → 404, which is safe; but the inverse (metadata key exists but DB slug differs) could write credentials with an appId that no service queries. Verify the slugs align; the double lookup is fragile.

findings.title: Sync endpoint request has no Content-Type header and no timeout; URLSearchParams body without header may be rejected or hang indefinitely
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends `body: new URLSearchParams({...})` but does not set `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. Per the fetch spec, when the body is a URLSearchParams object, fetch DOES set the content-type automatically — so that part is fine. However there is no `AbortSignal`/timeout: if the sync endpoint hangs, the token refresh (and therefore the booking flow that triggered it) hangs indefinitely. Also there is no `Authorization` header or signature — the endpoint must rely on network-level trust, which should be documented; and the endpoint URL is taken from env without validation (an `http://` URL would send user ids in cleartext). Add a timeout (AbortController), validate the URL scheme is https in production, and check `response.ok` before returning.

findings.title: Google refresh persists the full googleCredentials object but parseRefreshTokenResponse may have replaced refresh_token with the literal string 'refresh_token'
findings.body: Line 97: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` then line 98-101 persists `key`. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` sets `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (literal) when the parsed response lacks a refresh_token (see separate finding). Google's token refresh response typically omits `refresh_token` (it's only returned on first consent), so on the sync path — where the minimal schema only guarantees `access_token` — the stored credential's refresh_token is overwritten with the garbage literal `"refresh_token"`. The next refresh sends `refresh_token="refresh_token"` to Google → `invalid_grant` → the catch block at line 108 checks `message !== "invalid_grant"` and marks the credential `invalid: true`, permanently disconnecting the user's Google Calendar. This is a critical data-integrity bug in the primary calendar integration.

findings.title: Office365 getToken validates stored credential with refreshTokenResponseSchema which transforms expires_in into an absolute expiry, corrupting the stored shape on read
findings.body: Line 278: `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(o365AuthCredentials).success && !isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`. The schema (lines 51-57) transforms `expires_in` via `.transform((offset) => Math.round(+new Date()/1000 + offset))` — i.e., it converts a relative offset into an absolute timestamp. But `o365AuthCredentials` is the STORED credential where `expiry_date` holds the absolute expiry (set in the callback: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date()/1000 + responseBody.expires_in)`) and `expires_in` was deleted. So `safeParse` on the stored credential fails (no `expires_in`... actually `expires_in` is required in the schema — `expires_in: z.number().transform(...)` — and the stored credential has `expiry_date` not `expires_in`), meaning `getToken` ALWAYS takes the refresh path for Office365, refreshing on every call. Wait — the stored credential from the callback has `expiry_date` and no `expires_in`, so `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse` fails → `getToken` always refreshes → every calendar operation triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. This is a performance bug and, combined with the refresh-path issues above, breaks Office365. The validity check should use `expiry_date` (as `isExpired` does at line 279 — but it's gated behind the failed safeParse). The schema should be split into a 'stored credential' schema and a 'refresh response' schema.

findings.title: MS Teams isExpired uses millisecond timestamp against Date.now() but expiry_date is stored in milliseconds while Office365 calendar stores seconds — inconsistent units across the two adapters
findings.body: `const isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date());` — `+new Date()` is milliseconds. The callback (line 66 of callback.ts) sets `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)` — SECONDS plus offset, i.e. a seconds-based timestamp stored in `expiry_date`. So `expiry_date` (seconds, e.g. 1.7e9) is always far less than `Date.now()` (milliseconds, 1.7e12), making `isExpired` ALWAYS true → the token is refreshed on EVERY API call, and each refresh (per the sync-path bugs) can destroy the refresh token. This is a pre-existing unit mismatch (the callback stores seconds, the adapter compares against ms) that this PR's refresh changes amplify into a credential-destroying loop. Note the sibling `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` `isExpired` (line 235-241) compares `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` — seconds — but reads `o365AuthCredentials.expires_in` (line 279) which is a relative offset, not the absolute `expiry_date`... the two Office365 adapters are mutually inconsistent about which field holds the absolute expiry and in which unit.

findings.title: HubSpot isTokenValid logic is inverted: returns true when token is expired
findings.body: `const isTokenValid = (token: HubspotToken) => token && token.tokenType && token.accessToken && token.expiryDate && (token.expiresIn || token.expiryDate) < Date.now();` — the final condition is `< Date.now()`, meaning the function returns true only when the expiry is in the PAST (i.e., the token IS expired). Then line 210: `getToken: () => !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve([]) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. So when the token is expired, `isTokenValid` returns true → `!isTokenValid` is false → `refreshAccessToken` is called (correct by accident). When the token is VALID (expiry in the future), `isTokenValid` returns false → `!isTokenValid` is true → returns `Promise.resolve([])` — an empty array used as the token! This is inverted logic (pre-existing, not introduced by this PR, but the PR's refresh changes interact with it). The condition should be `> Date.now()` for validity. As written, valid tokens are never used and expired tokens trigger refresh — the net effect happens to work for refresh but `getToken` returning `[]` for valid tokens means `hubspotClient.setAccessToken` is never called with the valid token... actually `refreshAccessToken` calls `setAccessToken` at the end. This is fragile pre-existing logic that the PR should have fixed while touching this code.

findings.title: Zoho CRM isTokenValid is inverted (returns true when expired) — same class of bug as HubSpot
findings.body: `const isValid = token && token.access_token && token.expiryDate && token.expiryDate < Date.now();` — again `< Date.now()` means 'valid' only when expired. Line 244: `getToken: () => (isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve() : refreshAccessToken(credentialKey))`. When the token is expired, `isTokenValid` returns true → `getToken` resolves WITHOUT refreshing and WITHOUT setting `this.accessToken` (the `isTokenValid` body sets `this.accessToken = token.access_token` only when `isValid` is true, i.e., when expired — so it sets the EXPIRED token). When the token is valid (future expiry), `isTokenValid` returns false → triggers a refresh unnecessarily. The logic is inverted: it should be `token.expiryDate > Date.now()`. Net effect: Zoho CRM uses expired access tokens and refreshes valid ones — API calls fail with 401 until the credential happens to be refreshed by the inverted path. Pre-existing but directly in the code path this PR modifies.

findings.title: Zoom isTokenValid mixes expires_in (seconds offset) and expiry_date (ms timestamp) in a single comparison against Date.now()
findings.body: `const isTokenValid = (token: ZoomToken) => (token.expires_in || token.expiry_date) < Date.now();` — `expires_in` is a relative seconds offset (e.g. 3600) and `expiry_date` is an absolute ms timestamp. The expression prefers `expires_in` when present. The stored credential (from callback line 44-45) has `expiry_date` (ms) and `expires_in` DELETED (`delete responseBody.expires_in`), so `token.expires_in` is undefined and `expiry_date` (ms) is compared to `Date.now()` (ms) — correct. But the schema comment says `expires_in` is 'deprecated, purely for backwards compatibility', and old credentials may still have `expires_in` (a small number like 3600) → `3600 < Date.now()` is always true → token always considered valid → expired tokens are used → 401s. The function name/semantics are also inverted relative to usage at line 137 (`!isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? resolve(access_token) : refresh(...)`) — `isTokenValid` actually returns 'is expired'. Pre-existing confusion, but the PR's refresh changes rely on this check to decide when to call the (broken) sync path.

findings.title: Webex isTokenValid is inverted (returns true when expired)
findings.body: `const isTokenValid = (token: WebexToken) => token.expiry_date < Date.now();` — returns true when the token IS expired. Line 119-121: `return !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve(credentialKey.access_token) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. When expired: `isTokenValid` true → `!isTokenValid` false → refresh (correct by accident). When valid: `isTokenValid` false → `!isTokenValid` true → returns the access token (correct by accident). So despite the misleading name the net behavior is correct — but this is fragile and confusing; the function should be renamed `isTokenExpired` or the comparison flipped. Flagging as low severity since behavior is accidentally correct, but it's a trap for future edits in code this PR touches.

findings.title: No tests for the new webhook endpoint or the refresh/sync helpers
findings.body: The PR adds a new public API endpoint (`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`) that writes OAuth credentials, plus two new shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that are now on the token-refresh path of ~10 integrations. The PR description's checklist explicitly states 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works'. Given the number of shape-mismatch bugs identified in the refresh path (Response vs SDK response), unit tests for `refreshOAuthTokens` (both branches) and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (including the missing-refresh_token case) and integration tests for the webhook (auth, decryption, upsert race) are essential before merge.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse mutates its input argument and returns a SafeParseResult whose `.data` may be the minimum schema shape, losing provider-specific fields
findings.body: When the sync path is active, the function validates against `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (access_token + numeric props only) and returns that parsed data — dropping provider-specific fields like `token_type`, `scope`, `id`, `instance_url` that the strict schema would have required and that callers persist. For example `googlecalendar` line 97 passes the result to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` — wait, it passes `googleCredentials` (the merged object), so Google is ok. But `salesforce` line 90-99 persists `accessTokenParsed.data` directly as the credential key — on the sync path this would be the minimal shape `{ access_token, ...numbers }` plus the fabricated `refresh_token: "refresh_token"`, dropping `id`, `issued_at`, `signature`, `token_type`, `scope` that `salesforceTokenSchema` requires and that jsforce may need. The function should merge the minimal parse back into the original response object (preserving all fields) rather than returning the stripped parse result.

findings.title: Office365 refresh: handleErrorsJson on the sync-path Response parses the minimal sync JSON, then parseRefreshTokenResponse throws due to broken minimum schema, and the thrown error is unhandled
findings.body: Line 262: `const responseJson = await handleErrorsJson(response);` — on the sync path `response` is the sync endpoint's Response, so `responseJson` is the minimal `{ access_token, expiry }` object. Line 263 passes it to `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`. Because `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is broken (see separate finding — the computed-key syntax doesn't create an index signature), `safeParse` fails and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")`. This throw is NOT caught in `refreshAccessToken` (no try/catch), so it propagates through `getToken()` → `fetcher` → every Office365 calendar operation fails with an unhandled error when credential sync is enabled. The Office365 sync path is entirely broken.

findings.title: Lark refresh: sync-path Response from handleLarkError lacks the Lark envelope; data.data is undefined and credential is overwritten with undefined tokens
findings.body: Even if `handleLarkError` successfully parses the sync endpoint's minimal JSON `{ access_token, <expiry> }` (no Lark `{ code, data: {...} }` envelope), line 84-96 reads `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.access_token`, `data.data.expires_in` — all undefined because the sync response has no `data` envelope. Line 91-96 then builds `newLarkAuthCredentials` with `refresh_token: undefined`, `refresh_expires_date: NaN` (Math.round(+new Date()/1000 + undefined)), `access_token: undefined`, `expiry_date: NaN`, and line 98-105 persists this corrupted credential, destroying the user's Lark Calendar integration. The sync path for Lark is broken and destructive.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin refresh: sync-path minimal response lacks expires_in, producing NaN expiryDate; also refresh_token is overwritten with the old one but access_token shape mismatch
findings.body: On the sync path, `tokenInfo` is a fetch Response and `tokenInfo.data` is undefined → TypeError (see separate finding). But even if the shape were normalized to the sync JSON `{ access_token, expiry }`, line 98 computes `tokenInfo.data.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + tokenInfo.data.expires_in)` — the sync contract returns an absolute expiry, not a relative `expires_in`, so `expires_in` is undefined → `expiryDate = NaN`. Line 100 sets `refresh_token` to the old one (good), but `api_domain` and `accountServer` come from `credentialKey` (line 99 sets accountServer from credentialKey — ok), while `api_domain` is never set on the sync path → `token.api_domain` is undefined → all subsequent Bigin API URLs become `undefined/bigin/v1/...`. The Bigin sync refresh path produces a broken credential.

findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens silently falls back to the provider refresh when userId is null, but team/org credentials (teamId set, userId null) then bypass sync entirely with no indication
findings.body: The condition `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId)` means that when a credential belongs to a team (`credential.userId` is null, `teamId` set), the sync endpoint is NOT called and the provider refresh runs instead. For self-hosters using this feature, team credentials will silently diverge from the app store's source of truth — the app store cannot sync team credentials because the sync endpoint is keyed on `calcomUserId`. This may be intentional (the webhook only supports userId), but it is undocumented in the code and the PR description, and creates an inconsistency where some credentials sync and others don't. At minimum, document this limitation or extend the sync protocol to support teamId.

findings.title: Credential update overwrites the entire key, discarding fields the app may need (email, expiry_date, type-specific fields)
findings.body: The update path (lines 72-81) does `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id }, data: { key: keys } })` — replacing the entire `key` JSON with the webhook payload. For apps like Office365/Google whose credential key includes derived fields (`email`, `expiry_date`, `scope`, `token_type`), a sync payload containing only `{ access_token, refresh_token, ... }` will strip those fields. Downstream code that reads `credential.key.email` (e.g., calendar listing uses the stored email) or validates the full schema will break. The update should merge: `key: { ...existingCredential.key, ...keys }`, and ideally validate the merged result against the app's schema. The create path (line 83-90) has the same issue but is less severe.

findings.title: Salesforce credential update drops the old access_token fields and does not preserve refresh token rotation
findings.body: Line 96-99: `data: { key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token } }`. Salesforce's refresh response includes a new `access_token`, `signature`, `issued_at`, `id`, `instance_url`, `scope`, `token_type` — but NOT a new `refresh_token` (Salesforce refresh tokens are typically long-lived and not rotated on every refresh). The code correctly preserves the old refresh_token. However, it also means the update runs on EVERY getClient call (see separate finding), rewriting the credential each time. Additionally, if Salesforce ever DOES rotate the refresh token, this code would discard the new one. The update should only happen when the token actually changed, and should preserve any newly-returned refresh_token if present.

findings.title: MS Teams refresh computes expiry_date from expires_in which the sync endpoint does not return (it returns an absolute expiry), yielding expiry_date = Date.now()
findings.body: Line 84: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000);`. On the sync path, the endpoint returns an absolute expiry field (per the PR contract: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date') — there is no `expires_in`, so `expiry_date = Date.now() + 0` = now. Combined with the inverted `isExpired` check (always true, see separate finding), the token is refreshed on every call and the stored expiry is always 'now'. Even on the normal path, if Microsoft omits `expires_in` (it doesn't, but defensively), the same corruption occurs. The code should use the absolute expiry returned by the sync endpoint when present, falling back to computing from `expires_in`.

findings.title: Zoom refresh on sync path: minimal response lacks refresh_token, but key.refresh_token is overwritten with newTokens.refresh_token (undefined)
findings.body: Line 120: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token;`. On the sync path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` validates against the broken `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (see separate finding) — if it somehow passed, `newTokens` would be the minimal shape without `refresh_token`, so `key.refresh_token = undefined`, destroying the stored refresh token. Even on the normal path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` fabricates `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` when missing (Zoom DOES return a new refresh_token on refresh, so normal path is ok). But the sync path combined with the fabricated/missing refresh_token corrupts the credential. The update should preserve the existing refresh token when the response doesn't include one: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token ?? key.refresh_token`.

findings.title: Webex refresh overwrites refresh_token unconditionally; sync path (minimal response) would set it to undefined
findings.body: Line 101: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token;`. On the sync path, `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` requires `refresh_token` — so validation fails and the function rejects (see separate finding). But if the schema were relaxed for sync (as it should be), `newTokens.refresh_token` would be undefined and the stored refresh token would be destroyed. Webex rotates refresh tokens on use, so the normal path is fine, but the sync path must preserve the existing refresh token when the response omits it. Use `newTokens.refresh_token ?? key.refresh_token`.

findings.title: Google refresh on sync path never calls the provider, so googleCredentials.refresh_token is preserved but the sync endpoint's response is not merged into googleCredentials beyond access_token/expiry_date
findings.body: Lines 94-96: on the sync path, only `access_token` and `expiry_date` are copied from the (broken, see finding) token object into `googleCredentials`. The sync endpoint contract returns only those two fields, which is fine for Google. But because `res?.data` is undefined on the sync path (Response has no `.data`), the code throws before reaching this point (see the high-severity finding). Once that's fixed, this merge is correct for Google. No additional issue beyond the shape mismatch already reported.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is read at module scope in constants.ts but refreshOAuthTokens also checks process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT at call time — inconsistent gating between webhook and refresh paths
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` gates on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId`, while the webhook gates only on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`. This means a deployment can have the webhook enabled (secret + encryption key set) but no sync endpoint — in which case credentials can be pushed IN via webhook but token refreshes go direct to the provider. That's a valid configuration. Conversely, if `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set but the webhook secret is not, refreshes go to the sync endpoint but no credentials can be pushed — the sync endpoint becomes the only source of tokens, which may be intended. The asymmetry is worth documenting but is not a bug per se. Flagging as low/speculative — the main issue is that `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` doesn't include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, so the name is misleading.

findings.title: Webhook header name is configurable via env var, allowing an operator to accidentally weaken verification (e.g., set to a header an attacker controls like 'user-agent')
findings.body: `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]` — the header name is read from an environment variable with no validation. If an operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME=user-agent` (or any commonly-sent header), the 'secret' check compares the User-Agent header value to `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` — an attacker who knows the secret (or if it's weak) could pass verification by setting User-Agent. More realistically, a misconfiguration could make the check compare against a header that proxies set. The header name should be a hardcoded constant (or at least validated against a whitelist / not a standard header). The env var configurability adds risk without benefit.

findings.title: refreshTokenResponseSchema transforms expires_in into an absolute timestamp, but the same schema is used to validate the STORED credential in getToken where expires_in is absent and expiry_date holds the absolute value
findings.body: The schema at lines 51-57 requires `expires_in` (a relative offset) and transforms it to an absolute timestamp. It is used in two places with different data shapes: (1) line 263 to parse the refresh RESPONSE (which has `expires_in` — correct usage), and (2) line 278 to validate the STORED credential (`o365AuthCredentials`), which has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) and NO `expires_in` (deleted in the callback). The second usage always fails safeParse, making the validity check at line 278-281 always take the refresh path (see separate finding). The stored-credential validation should use a separate schema with `expiry_date: z.number()` and optional `expires_in`.

findings.title: HubSpot getToken returns Promise.resolve([]) (empty array) when token is 'valid' per inverted logic — downstream code receives an array instead of a token
findings.body: Line 210: `getToken: () => !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve([]) : refreshAccessToken(credentialKey.refreshToken)`. Due to the inverted `isTokenValid` (see separate finding), when the token is actually valid (future expiry), `isTokenValid` returns false, `!isTokenValid` is true, and `getToken` resolves to `[]` — an empty array, not a token. Callers (`createEvent` line 239: `await auth.getToken();`) ignore the return value and rely on `hubspotClient.setAccessToken` being called inside `refreshAccessToken`. So when the token is valid, `setAccessToken` is NEVER called and the hubspotClient uses whatever token was last set (possibly none) — API calls fail with 401. The inverted logic means valid tokens are never applied to the client. This is a pre-existing bug in the gating logic that the PR's changes interact with.

findings.title: Unrelated change: redirectUri hardcoded to 'zoho-bigin' instead of appConfig.slug
findings.body: The diff changes `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`;` to `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback`;`. If `appConfig.slug` is `zoho-bigin` this is a no-op refactor, but if the config slug ever differs (e.g., for a white-label variant), the hardcoded path breaks the OAuth redirect URI registration. This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and should be reverted to use `appConfig.slug` for consistency with the callback (which uses `appConfig.slug` at line 36).

findings.title: Fabricated refresh_token value 'refresh_token' is a magic string that will be sent to providers verbatim
findings.body: The literal string `"refresh_token"` used as a placeholder (line 26) is indistinguishable from a real (if unlikely) token value and will be sent to OAuth providers as `refresh_token="refresh_token"` after being persisted (see the high-severity finding on credential destruction). Even as a placeholder it should be obviously-invalid and, more importantly, the field should be left absent so callers can preserve the existing token. This is primarily a symptom of the deeper bug already reported; flagging the magic string explicitly.

findings.title: Three sequential DB queries (user, app, credential) could be reduced, and app metadata lookup duplicates the DB app check
findings.body: The handler performs `prisma.user.findUnique`, `prisma.app.findUnique`, then `prisma.credential.findFirst` sequentially. The user and app lookups are independent and could be parallelized with `Promise.all`. More importantly, the `prisma.app.findUnique` check is redundant with the `appStoreMetadata` lookup — if the slug exists in `appStoreMetadata`, the app is valid for credential purposes; the DB check only confirms the app is installed/enabled in this instance. If the intent is to ensure the app is enabled, the check should also verify the app is not disabled. As written, the three sequential round-trips add latency to a webhook that should be fast. Low severity (webhook volume is low) but worth noting.

findings.title: Pre-existing: getAvailability catch block logs and returns Promise.reject([]) — rejecting with an empty array instead of resolving
findings.body: Line 183-186: `catch (err) { console.log(err); return Promise.reject([]); }`. Rejecting with an empty array (not an Error) is an anti-pattern — callers awaiting this get a rejection whose reason is `[]`, which is truthy-checkable but not an Error instance, breaking error logging/handling upstream. This is pre-existing code not touched by the PR diff, but it's in a file heavily modified by the PR. Flagging as low since it's out of scope but a maintainer reviewing this file should note it.

findings.title: Salesforce parseRefreshTokenResponse throws on failure, making the `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` check at line 92 unreachable dead code
findings.body: Line 90: `const accessTokenParsed = parseRefreshTokenResponse(accessTokenJson, salesforceTokenSchema);` — but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` when `safeParse` fails (it never returns a `{success: false}` object). Line 92-94 `if (!accessTokenParsed.success) { return Promise.reject(...) }` is therefore unreachable — a parse failure surfaces as a thrown Error from `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, not as the intended Promise.reject. The thrown error propagates out of `getClient` (which is called in the constructor via `this.getClient(credential).then(...)`) resulting in an unhandled promise rejection in the constructor. The dead code indicates the contract mismatch between `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (throws) and its callers (expect SafeParseResult).

findings.title: Zoom refresh: handleZoomResponse on sync-path Response works, but the sync JSON lacks refresh_token/scope/token_type so zoomRefreshedTokenSchema fails and Zoom sync refresh always rejects
findings.body: On the sync path, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint Response. `handleZoomResponse(response, credential.id)` parses its JSON (the minimal `{ access_token, expiry }`). Line 104 validates with `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema)` — but `zoomRefreshedTokenSchema` (lines 66-72) requires `token_type: z.literal("bearer")`, `refresh_token: z.string()`, `expires_in: z.number()`, `scope: z.string()`. The minimal sync response has none of these, so validation fails and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' (or, if the broken minimum schema is used, the computed-key bug causes failure). Either way, Zoom token refresh via sync ALWAYS fails, and the thrown error propagates through `getToken()` breaking all Zoom meeting operations when sync is enabled. The sync path needs a relaxed schema that makes refresh_token/scope/token_type optional and preserves existing values.

findings.title: Webex refreshed-token schema requires refresh_token_expires_in which the sync endpoint does not return; sync path validation always fails
findings.body: Same class of issue as Zoom: `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (lines 49-56) requires `refresh_token: z.string()` and `refresh_token_expires_in: z.number()`. The sync endpoint returns only access token + expiry. On the sync path, `parsedToken.success` is false → line 89-91 rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' → Webex sync refresh always fails. The schema for the sync path must make these optional and preserve existing values from the stored credential (which the code already does at lines 99-105 by merging into `key`).

findings.title: MS Teams refresh: sync-path Response is passed to handleErrorsJson which expects a Response — ok — but the sync JSON lacks refresh_token, and the credential update at line 87-95 overwrites the entire key, losing refresh_token, email, scope, token_type
findings.body: Lines 87-95: `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: responseBody as unknown as Prisma.InputJsonValue } })`. `responseBody` on the sync path is the minimal `{ access_token, expiry }` JSON (plus the computed `expiry_date`). The stored credential previously contained `refresh_token`, `email`, `scope`, `token_type`, `ext_expires_in` (per the `O365AuthCredentials` interface, lines 27-35). The update REPLACES the entire key with the minimal object, so `refresh_token` becomes undefined. The next refresh reads `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token` (line 104) = undefined → sends `refresh_token=undefined` to Microsoft → invalid_grant → credential permanently broken. The update must merge: `key: { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...responseBody }` and preserve `refresh_token` when the response omits it.

findings.title: Pre-existing: Lark credential deletion on refresh-token expiry races with concurrent operations
findings.body: Line 62: `await prisma.credential.delete({ where: { id: credential.id } });` when the refresh token is expired. If two concurrent calendar operations trigger `refreshAccessToken` for the same credential, both may pass the expiry check and both attempt refresh/delete, or one deletes while the other is mid-API-call with the old token. This is pre-existing (not introduced by the PR), but the PR's changes to this function make the race more likely to surface (the sync path adds a network round-trip before the delete). Low severity; flagging for awareness since the PR modifies this exact function.

findings.title: Sync endpoint URL is not validated — an http:// URL would transmit calcomUserId in cleartext and allow MITM token injection
findings.body: `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` — the URL comes from an env var with no scheme validation. If an operator sets `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT=http://...` (e.g., for a local test), the user id is sent in cleartext and, more critically, the RESPONSE (which becomes the user's access token) can be tampered with by a network attacker — a full token-injection vector into the credential store. The function should reject non-https URLs (except perhaps localhost for development), or at minimum the documentation should mandate https. Given this endpoint returns live OAuth access tokens, enforcing https in production is important.

findings.title: Decrypted credential keys are written to the DB without re-encryption at rest validation, and the webhook accepts arbitrary JSON as the key
findings.body: The webhook decrypts `reqBody.keys` with `symmetricDecrypt` and writes the parsed JSON directly as `credential.key`. Cal.com stores credentials encrypted at rest via Prisma field encryption (PRISMA_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY) — but this handler writes the decrypted object through the standard Prisma client, which should apply field-level encryption transparently. However, there is no validation that the decrypted payload is a well-formed credential for the target app (see separate finding). From a security perspective, the webhook allows ANY holder of the webhook secret to write ANY JSON as ANY user's credential for ANY app — including overwriting a victim's Google Calendar credential with attacker-controlled tokens, effectively redirecting calendar data to an attacker-controlled account. The webhook secret is a powerful bearer token; the handler should at minimum validate the payload shape per app and consider scoping the secret or adding per-app authorization. Also, the decrypted plaintext keys exist in memory and are passed to Prisma — ensure they are not logged (the handler doesn't log them, which is good).

findings.title: Office365 refresh on sync path: the sync endpoint is called instead of Microsoft, but the response is parsed with handleErrorsJson which expects a fetch Response — the sync path returns a Response so this works, but the parsed JSON shape (minimal) fails refreshTokenResponseSchema which requires expires_in
findings.body: On the sync path, `response` is the sync endpoint's Response. `handleErrorsJson(response)` parses its JSON (minimal `{ access_token, expiry }`). `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)` — `refreshTokenResponseSchema` requires `expires_in: z.number()` (line 53). The sync contract returns an absolute expiry, not `expires_in`, so `safeParse` fails → `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws (see separate findings). The Office365 sync refresh path is broken. Additionally, even if it didn't throw, line 264 spreads `tokenResponse.data` (which would be the minimal shape) over `o365AuthCredentials`, and the `expires_in` transform would compute a wrong absolute value. The sync path needs a dedicated schema with an absolute expiry field.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes credentialId instead of userId to refreshOAuthTokens (duplicate of high finding, noting the exact line for the wrong argument)
findings.body: Line 93: `credentialId` is passed as the third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)`. The parameter is named `userId` in `refreshOAuthTokens` and is sent as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint. `credentialId` is the credential's primary key, not the user's id. This means the sync endpoint receives a credential id where it expects a user id — the self-hoster's app store will look up the wrong record (or fail), and tokens for the wrong user could be returned and written into this credential. This is the single most clear-cut correctness bug in the PR: every other caller passes `credential.userId`.

findings.title: HubSpot refresh: expiryDate computed from expiresIn which is undefined on the sync path, yielding NaN
findings.body: Line 192: `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn * 1000);`. On the sync path, `hubspotRefreshToken` is a fetch Response (see high-severity finding) — `expiresIn` is undefined → `expiryDate = NaN`. Even if the shape were normalized to the sync JSON, the sync contract returns an absolute expiry, not `expiresIn`, so `expiryDate` would still be NaN. The credential is then updated with `key: hubspotRefreshToken as any` containing `expiryDate: NaN`, and the inverted `isTokenValid` check (`(token.expiresIn || token.expiryDate) < Date.now()` → `NaN < Date.now()` → false) treats the token as valid forever, so the corrupted credential is never refreshed again. HubSpot sync path produces a permanently broken credential.

findings.title: Zoho CRM refresh hardcodes a 1-hour expiry (Date.now() + 60*60) instead of using the provider's expires_in
findings.body: Line 219: `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + 60 * 60);` — this hardcodes a 1-hour expiry regardless of what Zoho actually returns (`expires_in`). The callback (line 51 of callback.ts) does the same. On the sync path, the endpoint returns an absolute expiry which is ignored. If Zoho tokens last longer (they typically do), the credential is refreshed far more often than necessary (performance); if shorter, the token expires prematurely (correctness). This is pre-existing behavior, but the PR's sync changes should use the actual expiry from the response. Note `Date.now()` is ms and `expiryDate` is compared with `< Date.now()` in the inverted `isTokenValid` — units are consistent here (ms), unlike the Office365 adapters.

findings.title: Comment on isExpired is misleading given the unit mismatch with the callback
findings.body: Line 48 comment: '// Checks to see if our O365 user token is valid or if we need to refresh'. The function `isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date());` compares against milliseconds, but the callback stores `expiry_date` in SECONDS (line 66 of callback.ts: `Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)`). The comment doesn't document the unit, and the mismatch means `isExpired` always returns true. A maintainer reading this file would assume the check is correct. The units must be reconciled (either store ms in the callback or compare against seconds here) and documented.

findings.title: Google refresh catch block silently swallows non-invalid_grant errors and returns the auth client with a stale token, masking sync-path failures
findings.body: Lines 103-118: the catch block checks `if (message !== "invalid_grant") return myGoogleAuth;` — for ANY error other than invalid_grant (including the TypeError from the sync-path `.data` bug, network errors, or the 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' error from parseRefreshTokenResponse), it silently returns the auth client with the OLD expired credentials. The caller (`getToken` → `authedCalendar`) then makes API calls with an expired token, which fail with 401 from Google, surfacing as a confusing 'There was an error contacting google calendar service' error far from the root cause. Errors during refresh should be logged (via `this.log`) and, for non-invalid_grant errors, either rethrown or at least logged so operators can diagnose sync-path failures. The silent swallow makes the sync-path bugs (shape mismatch, fabricated refresh_token) nearly impossible to detect in production.

findings.title: Return type is `any` — the function returns either a provider SDK response object or a fetch Response, and TypeScript callers cannot distinguish
findings.body: `const refreshOAuthTokens = async (refreshFunction: () => any, appSlug: string, userId: number | null) => { ... return response; }` — the return type is inferred as `any` (union of the refreshFunction's return and Response). This is why the shape-mismatch bugs compiled without errors: callers assign the result to typed variables (`HubspotToken`, `res?.data`, etc.) and TypeScript doesn't complain because the function returns `any`. The function should have an explicit return type (e.g., `Promise<Response | Awaited<ReturnType<typeof refreshFunction>>>`) or, better, be redesigned to normalize the response shape so callers don't need to branch. The `any` type is the root enabler of the class of bugs found in this PR.

findings.title: Parameter `response: any` and `schema: z.ZodTypeAny` — no type safety on inputs
findings.body: The function signature `(response: any, schema: z.ZodTypeAny)` accepts anything. Combined with the `any` return type of `refreshOAuthTokens`, this creates a fully untyped pipeline for OAuth token data. The `response` parameter should be typed as `unknown` (forcing safeParse) and the return type should be `z.SafeParseReturnType<...>` or a discriminated union. The lack of types is why the Salesforce caller's `.success` check compiled despite the function throwing. Low severity on its own but contributes to the systemic issue.

findings.title: Stray empty JSDoc comment `/** */` above the handler
findings.body: Line 16: `/** */` — an empty JSDoc block left above `export default async function handler`. It serves no purpose and should be removed or replaced with a real description of the endpoint (method, auth, payload). Minor cleanup.

findings.title: Pre-existing: handleErrorJsonOffice365Calendar error condition `!response.ok && response.status < 200 && response.status >= 300` is always false
findings.body: Line 499: `if (!response.ok && response.status < 200 && response.status >= 300)` — `response.status < 200 && response.status >= 300` is a contradiction (no number is both < 200 and >= 300), so this condition is always false and the error branch (lines 500-501) is dead code. The intent was likely `response.status < 200 || response.status >= 300`. This is pre-existing and out of the PR's scope, but it's in a file the PR heavily modifies and it means Office365 error responses are not properly thrown. Flagging for maintainer awareness.

findings.title: Zoom getToken logic is inverted in naming: `!isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? resolve(access_token) : refresh(...)` — isTokenValid actually means 'is expired'
findings.body: `isTokenValid` (line 63) returns `(token.expires_in || token.expiry_date) < Date.now()` — true when the token IS expired. Line 137: `return !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve(credentialKey.access_token) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. When expired: `isTokenValid` true → `!isTokenValid` false → refresh (correct). When valid: `isTokenValid` false → `!isTokenValid` true → return access token (correct). So the net behavior is correct despite the inverted name, but the naming is a trap. Same pattern as Webex. Low severity; flagging because the PR modifies this function and a future edit could easily flip the logic.

findings.title: Lark getToken returns the access token string, but on the sync path refreshAccessToken returns newLarkAuthCredentials.access_token which may be undefined (sync response shape mismatch)
findings.body: Line 50-53: `getToken: () => !isExpired(larkAuthCredentials.expiry_date) ? Promise.resolve(larkAuthCredentials.access_token) : this.refreshAccessToken(credential)`. `refreshAccessToken` returns `newLarkAuthCredentials.access_token` (line 107). On the sync path, `newLarkAuthCredentials.access_token = data.data.access_token` where `data` is the parsed sync response — which has no Lark envelope, so `data.data` is undefined and `data.data.access_token` throws (see high-severity finding). If the shape were normalized, the sync response's `access_token` would be at the top level, not under `data`. The Lark sync path is broken at this level too.

findings.title: Office365 refresh persists o365AuthCredentials which on the sync path is the minimal response merged over the old credential — but the merge uses `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` which is dead code (parseRefreshTokenResponse throws), so on failure the OLD expired credential is persisted unchanged
findings.body: Line 264: `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`. Since `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on failure (never returns `{success: false}`), this line only executes on success. But note: `tokenResponse.data` on the sync path would be the minimal shape (access_token + numbers) — spreading it over `o365AuthCredentials` preserves old fields (good) but the `expires_in` transform in the schema would have converted the sync response's absolute expiry... actually the sync response has no `expires_in`, so the strict schema fails and the function throws. The merge logic itself is reasonable IF the parse succeeded, but the dead `.success` check means failures throw unhandled (see separate finding). Additionally, the persisted credential keeps the old `refresh_token` (good — it's in `o365AuthCredentials` and not overwritten by the minimal data), but loses nothing else. The main issue is the throw-on-failure contract mismatch.

findings.title: MS Teams refresh updates o365AuthCredentials in-memory (expiry_date, access_token) but the DB update writes responseBody which on the normal path includes the new refresh_token — however on the sync path responseBody lacks refresh_token so the DB loses it while the in-memory object keeps the old one, causing divergence
findings.body: Lines 87-98: the DB is updated with `key: responseBody` (the raw response body), while the in-memory `o365AuthCredentials` is updated with `expiry_date` and `access_token` from `responseBody` (lines 96-97). On the normal path, `responseBody` includes a new `refresh_token` (Microsoft rotates refresh tokens), so the DB gets the new one — consistent. On the sync path, `responseBody` has no `refresh_token`, so the DB loses it, but the in-memory `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token` still holds the old one — the in-memory object and the DB diverge. The next service instance loads the DB credential (no refresh_token) and refresh fails. The DB update should write the merged object (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...responseBody }`), not the raw responseBody.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin refresh preserves refresh_token from credentialKey (good) but on the sync path api_domain is not set, breaking all subsequent API URLs
findings.body: Line 99-100: `tokenInfo.data.accountServer = credentialKey.accountServer; tokenInfo.data.refresh_token = credentialKey.refresh_token;`. On the sync path, `tokenInfo.data` is the minimal sync JSON `{ access_token, expiry }` — it has no `api_domain`. The Bigin API URLs are built as `token.api_domain + this.contactsSlug` (line 137, 156, etc.). With `api_domain` undefined, all Bigin API calls go to `undefined/bigin/v1/...` and fail. The sync path must also preserve `api_domain` from the existing credential (like `accountServer` is preserved). The credential update at line 102-109 writes `key: tokenInfo.data as BiginToken` — missing `api_domain`, `scope`, `token_type` on the sync path.

findings.title: Zoho CRM refresh merges sync/normal response data over the old credential but hardcodes expiryDate to 1 hour, ignoring the actual token lifetime
findings.body: Lines 226-231: the DB update writes `{ ...(zohoCrmTokenInfo.data as ZohoToken), refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token, accountServer: credentialKey.accountServer }`. On the sync path, `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is undefined (Response has no `.data`) → TypeError (see high finding). Even if normalized, line 219 hardcodes `expiryDate = Date.now() + 60*60` (1 hour) regardless of the actual `expires_in` returned by Zoho or the absolute expiry returned by the sync endpoint. The `api_domain` field is also not preserved from `credentialKey` (unlike Bigin which preserves `accountServer`) — wait, `accountServer` IS preserved (line 229), but `api_domain` is not in the merge — on the sync path `api_domain` would be lost. Zoho CRM API URLs are hardcoded to `https://www.zohoapis.com/crm/v3/...` (lines 90, 105, 133, etc.) so `api_domain` isn't used for URLs in this service — ok, so that's fine. The main issue is the hardcoded 1-hour expiry and the shape mismatch.

findings.title: When userId is null (team credential), the sync endpoint is silently skipped — but the function still returns the provider refresh result, which is correct; however there is no logging or metric indicating sync was bypassed
findings.body: For team credentials (`credential.userId` is null), the sync endpoint is not called and the provider refresh runs. This is a silent behavioral difference: self-hosters enabling credential sync may expect ALL credentials to be synced, but team credentials silently diverge. There should be at least a debug log when sync is bypassed due to missing userId, so operators can diagnose why team credentials aren't syncing. Low severity / observability gap.

findings.title: User existence check queries the full user record when only existence is needed
findings.body: `prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: reqBody.userId } })` loads the entire user row (including potentially sensitive fields) just to check existence. `findUnique({ where: { id }, select: { id: true } })` or `count` would be sufficient and avoids loading unnecessary data into memory. Low severity for a webhook but a good practice, especially since the user object is not used beyond the null check.

findings.title: Google refresh persists `key` which is the SafeParseResult, not the parsed data — wait, parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the SafeParseResult object, and line 97 assigns it to `key`, then line 100 persists `data: { key }`
findings.body: Line 97: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` — `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns `refreshTokenResponse` which is the SafeParseResult (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), NOT the parsed data. Line 98-101: `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key } })` — this persists the SafeParseResult OBJECT (with `success` and `data` properties) as the credential key, not the actual token data! The credential key becomes `{ success: true, data: { access_token, refresh_token, ... } }` instead of `{ access_token, refresh_token, ... }`. Every subsequent read of `credential.key` (e.g., line 75 `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)`) will FAIL because the key has a `data` wrapper. This is a critical bug: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a SafeParseResult but the Google caller treats it as the parsed data. The caller should use `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` or the function should return `.data` directly. Note: the OLD code was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials);` which returned the parsed data directly — the refactor changed the return shape and broke the caller.

findings.title: Office365 refresh: tokenResponse is the SafeParseResult, and line 264 accesses tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data — this is correct usage IF parseRefreshTokenResponse returned a SafeParseResult, but it throws on failure (contract mismatch)
findings.body: Line 264: `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`. This caller correctly accesses `.success` and `.data` on the result — which would work IF `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returned a SafeParseResult. But `parseRefreshTokenResponse` THROWS on failure (see separate finding), so `tokenResponse` is always `{success: true, data}` when the function returns, and the `.success` check is always true. The spread works correctly on success. The issue is purely the throw-vs-return contract mismatch making the error handling dead. This caller is actually written correctly for the INTENDED contract — the function doesn't honor it.

findings.title: Zoom refresh: `newTokens = parsedToken.data` — parsedToken is the SafeParseResult from parseRefreshTokenResponse, so .data is correct here; but if parseRefreshTokenResponse throws (which it does on failure), the explicit `if (!parsedToken.success)` check at line 108 is unreachable
findings.body: Line 104: `const parsedToken = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema);` — returns SafeParseResult on success, throws on failure. Line 108: `if (!parsedToken.success)` — always false when reached (since failure throws). Line 111: `const newTokens = parsedToken.data;` — correct on success. The dead check is the issue (see separate finding on the contract mismatch). The Zoom caller is written for the intended contract; the function doesn't honor it.

findings.title: Salesforce credential update spreads accessTokenParsed.data (SafeParseResult.data) — correct on success, but on the sync path the minimal schema strips provider-specific fields
findings.body: Line 98: `data: { key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token } }`. On the normal path, `accessTokenParsed.data` is the full Salesforce token (validated by `salesforceTokenSchema` which requires id, issued_at, instance_url, signature, access_token, scope, token_type) — good. On the sync path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` validates against the broken `minimumTokenResponseSchema` and returns the minimal shape — dropping `id`, `issued_at`, `signature`, `scope`, `token_type`, `instance_url`... wait, the minimum schema requires `access_token` and allows other properties via the (broken) index signature. If the index signature worked, it would passthrough all properties. But since the computed-key syntax is broken (see separate finding), the parse FAILS and the function throws. So on the sync path, Salesforce refresh throws 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' — the Salesforce sync path is broken at the schema level.
