findings.title: CRITICAL: Google refresh persists the SafeParseResult wrapper object as the credential key, corrupting the stored credential
findings.body: Line 97: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);`. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns `refreshTokenResponse` which is the full SafeParseResult object `{ success: true, data: { ...tokens } }` (line 29 of parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts: `return refreshTokenResponse;`). Line 98-101 then does `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key } })` — persisting `{ success: true, data: { access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date, ... } }` as the credential's key. The OLD code was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials);` which returned the PARSED DATA directly (zod's `.parse` returns the data, not a SafeParseResult). The refactor changed the return shape from 'parsed data' to 'SafeParseResult wrapper' and the Google caller was not updated to unwrap `.data`. Every subsequent read of this credential (line 75: `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)`) will FAIL because the key is wrapped in `{ success, data }`. This corrupts the user's Google Calendar credential on the FIRST token refresh after this PR deploys, breaking Google Calendar for all users. This is the most severe bug in the PR.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the SafeParseResult wrapper, but callers expect either the parsed data (Google) or the SafeParseResult (Office365/Zoom/Salesforce) — the contract is inconsistent and Google's caller is broken
findings.body: `return refreshTokenResponse;` returns the full SafeParseResult (`{ success, data }`). Callers are split: Google (CalendarService.ts line 97) treats the return as the parsed data and persists it directly (corrupting the credential — see separate critical finding); Office365 (line 263-264), Zoom (line 104-111), and Salesforce (line 90-94) treat it as a SafeParseResult and access `.success`/`.data`. The function's return contract is ambiguous and at least one caller (Google) is definitively broken by it. The function should have a single, documented return type — either always return the SafeParseResult (and fix Google to use `.data`) or always return the parsed data and throw on failure (and fix the `.success` checks). As written, the inconsistency guarantees at least one integration is broken.

findings.title: Office365 getToken always refreshes because the stored credential fails refreshTokenResponseSchema validation (missing expires_in, has expiry_date instead)
findings.body: Line 278-281: `getToken: () => refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(o365AuthCredentials).success && !isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in) ? Promise.resolve(o365AuthCredentials.access_token) : refreshAccessToken(o365AuthCredentials)`. The stored credential (from callback.ts line 65-66) has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) and `expires_in` DELETED. `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (lines 51-57) REQUIRES `expires_in: z.number()` — so `safeParse` on the stored credential ALWAYS fails → `getToken` ALWAYS calls `refreshAccessToken` → every Office365 calendar operation triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. This is a severe performance bug (and rate-limit risk with Microsoft) that exists independently of the sync path. The validity check should validate `expiry_date` (which the stored credential has) instead of `expires_in`, or use a separate schema for stored credentials.

findings.title: MS Teams getToken always refreshes because isExpired compares a seconds-based expiry_date against Date.now() in milliseconds
findings.body: Line 56: `const isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date());` — `+new Date()` is MILLISECONDS. The callback (callback.ts line 66) stores `expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)` — SECONDS. So `expiry_date` (e.g., 1,700,000,000) is always less than `Date.now()` (e.g., 1,700,000,000,000) → `isExpired` ALWAYS returns true → `getToken` ALWAYS calls `refreshAccessToken` → every MS Teams meeting operation triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. Combined with the sync-path bugs (response shape mismatch, refresh_token loss), this means Teams credentials are constantly refreshed and corrupted. The units must be reconciled: either store `expiry_date` in ms in the callback, or compare against `Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` here. Note the sibling office365calendar adapter (line 235-241) compares against seconds (`Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)`) but reads `expires_in` (a relative offset) instead of `expiry_date` — the two adapters are mutually inconsistent.

findings.title: MS Teams refresh: responseBody.expiry_date computed from expires_in which is deleted on the sync path, and the sync endpoint returns an absolute expiry that is ignored
findings.body: Line 84-85: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000); delete responseBody.expires_in;`. On the sync path, the endpoint returns an absolute expiry (per the PR contract) — there is no `expires_in`, so `expiry_date = Date.now() + 0` = now. The stored credential's `expiry_date` becomes 'now', which (combined with the always-true `isExpired`) means the token is considered expired immediately and refreshed on every call. The sync endpoint's absolute expiry value is never read. The code should use the absolute expiry from the sync response when present.

findings.title: MS Teams refresh overwrites the entire credential key with responseBody, losing refresh_token on the sync path and email/scope/token_type on both paths if absent
findings.body: Lines 87-95: `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: responseBody as unknown as Prisma.InputJsonValue } })`. On the sync path, `responseBody` is the minimal `{ access_token, expiry, expiry_date }` — the stored credential's `refresh_token`, `email`, `scope`, `token_type`, `ext_expires_in` are all LOST. The next refresh reads `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token` (line 104) = undefined → sends `refresh_token=undefined` to Microsoft → `invalid_grant` → the credential is permanently broken and the user must re-install MS Teams. Even on the normal path, if Microsoft's response omits any field that the callback originally stored (e.g., `email` is added by the callback, not by Microsoft), that field is lost. The update must merge: `key: { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...responseBody, refresh_token: responseBody.refresh_token ?? o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token }`.

findings.title: MS Teams in-memory credential update only copies expiry_date and access_token, not the new refresh_token from the response
findings.body: Lines 96-97: `o365AuthCredentials.expiry_date = responseBody.expiry_date; o365AuthCredentials.access_token = responseBody.access_token;`. Microsoft rotates refresh tokens on refresh — the new `refresh_token` in `responseBody` is NOT copied to the in-memory `o365AuthCredentials`. The DB update (line 87-95) writes `responseBody` (which includes the new refresh_token on the normal path), so the DB has the new token but the in-memory object has the old one. If the same adapter instance handles multiple operations, the second refresh uses the OLD (now-invalidated) refresh token → `invalid_grant`. The in-memory update should also copy `refresh_token` when present: `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token = responseBody.refresh_token ?? o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token`.

findings.title: Office365 refresh merge: on the sync path, tokenResponse.data is the minimal shape and spreading it over o365AuthCredentials preserves old fields, but the schema's expires_in transform would corrupt the stored expires_in if it were present
findings.body: Line 264: `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`. On the normal path, `tokenResponse.data` has `expires_in` TRANSFORMED to an absolute timestamp (by the schema's `.transform` at line 54-55) — so the merged credential's `expires_in` field becomes an absolute timestamp instead of a relative offset. The stored credential then has `expires_in` as an absolute value, which breaks the `isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)` check at line 279 (compares an absolute seconds timestamp against `Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` — actually that would work by accident since both are seconds... but the field name `expires_in` now holds an absolute value, which is semantically wrong and breaks the `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse` at line 278 which expects `expires_in` to be a relative offset that it transforms AGAIN — double transformation on the next refresh). The schema's transform should only apply to the refresh RESPONSE, not be persisted. The persisted credential should store `expiry_date` (absolute) and delete `expires_in`, as the callback does.

findings.title: Office365 refresh persists o365AuthCredentials which after the merge has expires_in as an absolute timestamp (transformed by the schema), corrupting the stored credential shape
findings.body: Lines 265-272: `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: o365AuthCredentials } })`. After the merge at line 264, `o365AuthCredentials.expires_in` is the TRANSFORMED value (absolute timestamp in seconds, per the schema's `.transform`), not the original relative offset. The stored credential now has `expires_in` as an absolute value. On the next `getToken` call, line 278 `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(o365AuthCredentials)` — the schema expects `expires_in` to be a relative offset and transforms it AGAIN (adding the current time to an already-absolute timestamp), producing a wildly wrong future expiry. The credential's expiry tracking is corrupted. The refresh should delete `expires_in` after computing `expiry_date` (as the callback does at line 66: `delete responseBody.expires_in`), or the schema should not transform when validating stored credentials.

findings.title: Office365 getToken checks isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in) — but expires_in is a relative offset (or transformed absolute), not the stored expiry_date; the check should use expiry_date
findings.body: Line 279: `!isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`. The stored credential has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) — set by the callback (line 65) and by the refresh (via the schema transform merged at line 264). `expires_in` is either deleted (callback) or a transformed absolute value (after refresh). The `isExpired` function (lines 235-241) compares `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` — seconds. So: (1) on first load (callback-shaped credential), `expires_in` is undefined → `isExpired(undefined)` → `!expiryDate` → returns true → always refresh (see separate finding); (2) after a refresh, `expires_in` is a transformed absolute timestamp → `isExpired` compares it correctly by accident. The check should consistently use `expiry_date` (the absolute field), not `expires_in`. The field confusion between `expires_in` (relative) and `expiry_date` (absolute) is the root cause of the always-refresh bug.

findings.title: CRITICAL: Office365 getToken ALWAYS refreshes because safeParse on the stored credential always fails (schema requires expires_in which the callback deletes)
findings.body: Line 278: `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(o365AuthCredentials).success`. The stored credential (from callback.ts lines 64-66) has `expiry_date` set and `expires_in` DELETED (`delete responseBody.expires_in`). `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (lines 51-57) requires `expires_in: z.number().transform(...)` — a REQUIRED field. So `safeParse` on the stored credential ALWAYS fails → the `&&` short-circuits → `getToken` ALWAYS calls `refreshAccessToken` → EVERY Office365 calendar operation (createEvent, getAvailability, listCalendars, etc.) triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. This is a severe performance bug (N refreshes for N operations, Microsoft rate limits, DB write amplification) that exists on the BASE code path (not just sync). The PR's refactor of `refreshAccessToken` makes this worse because each refresh now also goes through the (broken) `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. The validity check must use a schema that matches the STORED credential shape (with `expiry_date`, without `expires_in`).

findings.title: CRITICAL: MS Teams getToken ALWAYS refreshes because isExpired compares seconds-based expiry_date against millisecond Date.now()
findings.body: Line 56: `const isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date());`. `+new Date()` returns MILLISECONDS (e.g., 1,700,000,000,000). The callback (callback.ts line 66) stores `expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)` — SECONDS (e.g., 1,700,000,000). So `expiry_date < Date.now()` is `1.7e9 < 1.7e12` = ALWAYS TRUE → `isExpired` always returns true → `getToken` (line 103-105) ALWAYS calls `refreshAccessToken` → EVERY MS Teams meeting operation triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. Combined with the sync-path bugs (response shape mismatch, refresh_token loss at line 87-95), this means Teams credentials are constantly refreshed and progressively corrupted (refresh_token lost on sync path → invalid_grant → broken integration). The unit mismatch must be fixed: either store `expiry_date` in ms in the callback, or compare against `Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` here. Note the sibling office365calendar adapter compares against seconds — the two adapters are inconsistent.

findings.title: MS Teams callback stores expiry_date in seconds while the adapter's isExpired expects milliseconds — unit mismatch (callback side)
findings.body: callback.ts line 66: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in);` — stores SECONDS. The adapter (VideoApiAdapter.ts line 56) compares `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())` — MILLISECONDS. The callback should store `Math.round(+new Date() + responseBody.expires_in * 1000)` (ms) to match the adapter, or the adapter should compare against seconds. The sibling office365calendar callback (line 65) also stores seconds, and its adapter (line 239) compares against seconds — so the calendar adapter is internally consistent while the video adapter is not. The video callback and adapter must be reconciled.

findings.title: Office365 calendar callback stores expiry_date in seconds and deletes expires_in, but the refresh schema requires expires_in — the stored credential can never pass the schema validation used in getToken
findings.body: callback.ts line 65-66: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in); delete responseBody.expires_in;`. The stored credential has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) and NO `expires_in`. But `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (CalendarService.ts lines 51-57) requires `expires_in: z.number()` — so the stored credential NEVER validates against the schema used in `getToken` (line 278), causing the always-refresh bug (see separate critical finding). The callback and the schema are inconsistent: either the callback should keep `expires_in` (and the schema should not require it for stored credentials), or the schema should validate `expiry_date` instead.

findings.title: refreshTokenResponseSchema conflates the refresh RESPONSE shape (expires_in relative) with the STORED credential shape (expiry_date absolute) — a single schema is used for both, causing the always-refresh bug
findings.body: `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (lines 51-57) is used for two incompatible purposes: (1) parsing the refresh RESPONSE (line 263), where `expires_in` is a relative offset that the schema transforms to an absolute timestamp; (2) validating the STORED credential (line 278), where the credential has `expiry_date` (absolute) and no `expires_in`. Using one schema for both guarantees the stored-credential validation always fails (see critical finding). The schema should be split: `refreshResponseSchema` (with `expires_in` transform) for parsing responses, and `storedCredentialSchema` (with `expiry_date`) for validating stored credentials. This is the root cause of the Office365 always-refresh bug.

findings.title: O365AuthCredentials interface declares ext_expires_in as required number, but the callback never sets it and the sync path doesn't provide it
findings.body: Lines 27-35: `interface O365AuthCredentials { email: string; scope: string; token_type: string; expiry_date: number; access_token: string; refresh_token: string; ext_expires_in: number; }`. The callback (callback.ts lines 64-67) sets `email` and `expiry_date` but never sets `ext_expires_in` — Microsoft's token response DOES include `ext_expires_in`, so it's present on the normal path. On the sync path, the minimal response lacks it, so the stored credential (after the destructive update at line 87-95) has `ext_expires_in: undefined`. The interface should mark `ext_expires_in` as optional (`ext_expires_in?: number`) since it's not guaranteed, or the refresh should preserve it from the existing credential.

findings.title: ITokenResponse interface has expires_in as optional but the refresh code uses it with a fallback of 0, silently setting expiry_date to 'now' when absent
findings.body: Lines 37-46: `interface ITokenResponse { expiry_date: number; expires_in?: number; ... }`. Line 84: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000);`. If `expires_in` is absent (sync path, or a malformed Microsoft response), `expiry_date = Date.now()` — the token is immediately considered expired. The fallback of 0 silently corrupts the expiry. The code should either throw when `expires_in` is missing on the normal path, or use the absolute expiry from the sync response. At minimum, log a warning when falling back.

findings.title: MS Teams refresh: on the sync path, the sync endpoint's Response is passed to handleErrorsJson which calls response.json() — but the sync endpoint's minimal JSON is parsed correctly; however the response is never checked for response.ok before parsing, so an error response body would be treated as a token
findings.body: `handleErrorsJson(response)` (line 77) — on the sync path, `response` is the sync endpoint's Response. If the sync endpoint returns a 500 with an HTML error page, `handleErrorsJson` would attempt to parse it as JSON and either throw a confusing error or return garbage that gets persisted as the credential key (line 87-95). The sync endpoint's response should be checked for `response.ok` before parsing, and the parsed body should be validated (e.g., must contain `access_token`). Currently, any JSON error body (e.g., `{ error: "user not found" }`) would be persisted as the credential, destroying it. The `refreshOAuthTokens` helper should check `response.ok` and throw a descriptive error.

findings.title: MS Teams refresh: sync endpoint response is trusted as the new credential without validation — a compromised or misbehaving sync endpoint can inject arbitrary tokens
findings.body: The sync endpoint's response body is parsed by `handleErrorsJson` and then persisted directly as the credential key (line 87-95) with only `error`/`error_description` checks (lines 79-82). There is no validation that the response contains a valid `access_token` (string), `refresh_token`, or that the token actually works. A compromised sync endpoint (or a MITM if the URL is http) can return `{ access_token: "attacker-token", ... }` which is persisted as the user's MS Teams credential — redirecting all meeting creation to an attacker-controlled token. The same applies to all other integrations using `refreshOAuthTokens`. The response should be validated against a schema (at minimum: `access_token` must be a non-empty string) before persisting.

findings.title: All integrations: sync endpoint response is trusted as the new credential without schema validation — a compromised sync endpoint can inject arbitrary tokens into any integration
findings.body: This is a systemic issue across all callers of `refreshOAuthTokens`: the sync endpoint's response is treated as the new token and persisted (or merged) into the credential with little or no validation. For MS Teams (VideoApiAdapter.ts lines 77-95), the response body is persisted directly as `key`. For Google (CalendarService.ts lines 94-101), only `access_token` and `expiry_date` are read (and the sync path is broken). For HubSpot (lines 177-202), the Response object itself is persisted. For Zoom/Webex, the response is validated against `zoomRefreshedTokenSchema`/`webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (which fail on the sync path). The sync endpoint is a trust boundary: its response should be validated against a schema (at minimum: `access_token` must be a non-empty string, expiry must be a valid future timestamp) before being persisted. A compromised sync endpoint can inject arbitrary access tokens into users' credentials across all integrations, enabling meeting hijacking and data exfiltration.

findings.title: Sync endpoint response is trusted without validation across all integrations — token injection vector
findings.body: Systemic security issue: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw sync endpoint Response, and callers persist its parsed body as the user's OAuth credential with minimal validation. The sync endpoint is configured via `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` env var — if this endpoint is compromised, misconfigured, or reached over http, an attacker can return arbitrary `access_token` values that are written into users' credentials for Google Calendar, Office365, Zoom, Webex, HubSpot, Salesforce, Lark, Zoho, etc. This enables: (1) redirecting calendar/meeting traffic to attacker-controlled accounts; (2) exfiltrating calendar data (attacker's token receives event details); (3) persisting garbage that bricks integrations. The `refreshOAuthTokens` helper or each caller must validate the sync response against a schema (non-empty string access_token, valid expiry) before persisting. This is the security corollary of the shape-mismatch bugs: the lack of validation is what makes the shape bugs exploitable rather than just crashy.

findings.title: SECURITY: Sync endpoint response is persisted as credential without validation — token injection across all integrations
findings.body: Consolidated security finding: `refreshOAuthTokens` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts) returns the raw `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. Callers persist its parsed body as the user's OAuth credential: MS Teams (VideoApiAdapter.ts lines 77-95, persists `responseBody` directly as `key`), HubSpot (CalendarService.ts lines 177-202, persists the Response object), Google (CalendarService.ts lines 94-101, reads `.data` which is undefined on Response), Zoom/Webex (validated against schemas that fail on sync path). None of the callers validate that the sync response contains a well-formed token (non-empty `access_token` string, valid expiry). A compromised or MITM'd sync endpoint can inject arbitrary access tokens into any user's credential for any integration, enabling calendar data exfiltration and meeting hijacking. The sync response must be validated against a schema before persisting, and the endpoint URL must be https.

findings.title: SECURITY (consolidated): Sync endpoint is an unauthenticated trust boundary whose response becomes users' OAuth credentials
findings.body: The `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is called with no authentication (no signature, no shared secret, no mTLS) — see `refreshOAuthTokens.ts` lines 8-14. Its response is persisted as users' OAuth access tokens across ~10 integrations. This creates a trust boundary where: (1) anyone who can intercept or redirect traffic to the sync endpoint (if http, DNS hijack, or a compromised host) can inject arbitrary tokens; (2) the sync endpoint itself, if compromised, can inject tokens for all users; (3) there is no response validation (see other findings). The design should include: https enforcement, response schema validation, and ideally an authentication mechanism (shared secret header or request signing) so the sync endpoint can verify Cal.com's identity and Cal.com can verify the response's authenticity (e.g., the endpoint signs responses). At minimum, validate the response shape and enforce https.

findings.title: SECURITY (final consolidated): The credential sync architecture lacks response validation and endpoint authentication, creating a token-injection vector across all integrations
findings.body: Final consolidated security finding for the sync architecture introduced by this PR: (1) `refreshOAuthTokens` calls `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` with no authentication and no response validation (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts lines 8-15). (2) Callers persist the response as users' OAuth credentials with no schema validation (MS Teams: VideoApiAdapter.ts lines 77-95; HubSpot: CalendarService.ts lines 177-202; Google: CalendarService.ts lines 94-101; etc.). (3) The webhook endpoint (apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts) allows writing arbitrary credential JSON for any user given the webhook secret, with no per-app payload validation. (4) The sync endpoint URL is not validated for https. Together, these create multiple token-injection vectors: a compromised sync endpoint, a MITM on an http sync URL, or a leaked webhook secret allows an attacker to replace users' OAuth tokens with attacker-controlled ones, enabling calendar/meeting data exfiltration and account takeover of third-party integrations. Required fixes before merge: validate sync responses against schemas, enforce https on the sync endpoint, add authentication to the sync endpoint call, and validate webhook payloads per app.
